BORDER BALLS UP - COVID Fence Revamp

By: Nicky Troll | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
a multi-million rand border repair project between Zim & SA has opened the gates for opportunistic for smugglers - we investigate

Unique Selling Point:
* current news
* mismanagement of government funding
* criminals at work
* present on the ground

Further information:
Construction of a new fence at the Beitbridge border between South Africa and Zimbabwe will begin this week and be completed within 40 days, public works minister Patricia de Lille said on Thursday.
"In terms of Section 27 (2) (l) of the Disaster Management Act, No. 57 of 2002, I have invoked emergency procurement procedures in relation to the erection and repairs of the border fences, east and west of the (Beitbridge) border post," De Lille said at the time.
The step followed President Cyril Ramaphosa’s address to the nation when he declared a national State of Disaster in response to the Covid-19 pandemic, saying the country's borders would be secured, and the Department of Defence had asked that the fence be repaired for the shutdown.
However, in May, De Lille said the newly erected fence had been damaged, and that units of the SANDF were being deployed to the border.
The R37m fence at the Beitbridge border separating SA and Zimbabwe was hardly up a day before trespassers cut through it to smuggle in contraband.
And the presence of military personnel along the border has done little to repel desperate Zimbabweans and criminals from crossing over to this country.
“The fence was hardly up for one day and the crooks came through with cases of cigarettes and smuggling food, and all of that,” an exasperated Patricia de Lille told MPs on Monday.
The public works and infrastructure minister told MPs that the auditor-general confirmed on Thursday that he will investigate whether SA got value for money from the project and whether due processes were followed in appointing the contractor to erect the fence.
“But it's going to take longer due to the lockdown,” De Lille was told.
“What must be condemned in the strongest possible terms is the criminality that is taking place in our borders. The crooks are always one [step] ahead of us and where we were asked to replace the fence was specifically where they call it the hotspots.”
She said she asked defence minister Nosiviwe Mapisa-Nqakula on April 4, to make the SA national defence force available to patrol the fence regularly.
“Even that is not helping,” said De Lille.
“They are watching them. The SANDF is there on bikes, they drive up there, but the crooks just know where and when to strike. It is big problem at our borders that we need to address going into the future to make sure with the help of other countries, we secure the borders of SA,” she added.
It was the first time that a parliamentary committee discussed the controversial fence which was erected as a measure to fight the spread of coronavirus.
An audit into the procurement process of the Beitbridge border fence is underway.

The Public Works and Infrastructure Department says it has already paid around R21-million for the fence.

But pictures of the damaged fence has been making the rounds on social media.
Officials have reported problems of vandalism. The project is estimated to cost R37-million while the actual cost of the fence will be determined when the project is complete.

We interview Security Expert working on the border, the CPF chairperson and two Zim smugglers bringing food and smokes.

STRUCTURE: BORDER BALLS UP

VO: COVID-19 brought the world to a halt with international travel bans around the globe. Points of entry have been closed off to nonessential human traffic - a move that’s intensified the challenges at South Africa’s porous borders.

JAKKIE: South Africa has a serious border security challenge. // we simply don't have the capacity or the budget INT2M1

VO: Beitbridge in Musina, Limpopo is the only formal border post on the 225 kilometer line separating Zimbabwe and South Africa – but it is not the only crossing point.

LINK: This border is crossed illegally every single day people in search of better opportunities smugglers transporting illicit goods from cigarettes to basic essentials like food. In the time of COVID 19 desperate times call for desperate measures.

VO: This is a video of a group of people moving groceries across the Limpopo River illegally. Listen as a man hurries them along.

UPSOUND CLIP (CELLPHONE CLIP MUSINA EXPRESS DURATION 1.10)
MAN: Move quickly! The soldiers are going to catch you here, move to the other side! [TIMECODE: 0.4 to 0.7]

VO: Not everyone who crosses the border illegally is motivated by crime. For many it’s a matter of survival, with food prices skyrocketing in Zimbabwe. This man helps people smuggle food out of South Africa.

SMUGGLER: // more people and more actually more groceries. Because sometime xxxx maybe 10 bakkie crossing from Musina to here. M7

VO: In a rush to seal off borders amidst the growing COVID-19 crisis, the Department of Public Works and Infrastructure awarded a R37 million border fence repair contract to Magwa Construction in March this year.

Minister of the Department, Patricia de Lille spoke to us via Skype from Cape Town.

DE LILLE: that was to make sure that we protect. South Africans against COVID 19 and also people coming into our country. M2

VO: While the intention was great, it appears the implementation was not so great – because people are still crossing in and out of South Africa illegally.

HERMANUS: people are running down up and down and none of them had hand sanitizer or masks. INT3M3

VO: Hermanus Schoeman’s land borders the servitude road that runs along the fence, he also owns a local security company that was contracted to guard part of the fence during the construction phase.

HERMANUS: // if you look at the material that was used and the way it was designed and is it's not the best it's not a secure fence. It's not what you would expect between two countries. INT3M2

LINK: This is the result of the border fence project 40 kilometers of fence at one point eight meters high consisting of a grid of rolls and coiled razor wire. It works out to about a million rand per kilometer. Some would argue it's a steep price for something that's clearly not serving its purpose.

VO: Jakkie Cilliers of the Institute for Security Studies explains a fence without visible patrolling is meaningless.

JAKKIE: // Ill conceived poorly executed with no. No degree of planning or thinking about what is the intent.
MAC: // It's actually not a deterrent.
JAKKIE: No not at all. I can go and cut the fence and move through nothing will stop me.//. Int2M8

VO: And that’s exactly what’s happening.

SMUGGLER: People are cutting the fence too much // I find maybe 20 t0 30, 35 holes // INT2M10
MAC: // how are the guys actually getting through this fence.
HERMANUS: Oh very easy..// They go with a plyer I've got cut, cut, cut and been open and walk through it yes. INT3M1

LINK: There's nothing subtle about this. They've cut a man sized hole in a 37 million rand fence. And this is literally three kilometers from the first military base.

SMUGGLER: Those people cutting the fence //Is only the smugglers the cigarette smugglers. They scared of the soldiers // that’s why they cut // M5
MAC: Are they dangerous?
SMUGGLER: Let me say. Yes because those guys tey carry
MAC: Firearems
SMUGGLER Guns, ey, lot of things INT2M7

VO: The food smuggler claims he doesn’t cut the fence – he goes though an access gate used by landowners to reach water pumps on the Limpopo River. Passports don’t get stamped and the crossing is still illegal explains Cilliers.

JAKKIE: // there is an. Never ending stream and movement of people. // smuggling networks of mushroom and they very easily traverse across these borders // INT2M3 // // smuggling goods not only into South Africa but out of South Africa. That includes contraband // Int2M6

VO: Watch as these men carry cartons and cartons of cigarettes on their backs.

It’s a lucrative business. With millions to be made - smugglers come armed and ready to shoot to protect their goods.

Locals are scared and choose to rather turn a blind eye in fear of retribution. This is a Farm Manager from Musina. He’s seen smugglers move across the farm – sometimes in broad daylight – and now, more than ever before.

MORNE: / they more than 16-20 guys // the front guy the back guy is normally walking with some R4 these nine mils and guns that they're using so that they protect the guys walking between them. INT1 M8 normally we leave them because if it's cigarettes I mean as a farmer they target you as well. INT1M7
VO: It’s organised syndicates at work, according to Schoeman. He says, when the runners aren’t escorted by gunwielding guards - they often pay for protection.

HERMANUS: // I saw guys coming through with bags. I saw the military guys catching them. I saw the military guys releasing them. We went down we go one of the guys with the cigarette bags and he told us that they had to pay the military six hundred rand each to come through with their cigarettes //. ITN1M12
VO: But besides the criminality, people are flooding in and out of South Africa – defeating the purpose of COVID travel bans.

JAKKIE: The South African government rushed into building a fence and doing something to be seen to do to to take action // this is an example of. a vanity project that serves no intent. Int3M4

VO: Questions have been raised over whether the project was necessary, whether it was priced correctly and whether the contract was awarded fairly.

With public concern around the project mounting, Minister De Lille halted payments to the contractor, Magwa Construction. At that stage, the company had already been paid R21 million.

DE LILLE: where there's smoke there's fire. M10 the public has got their right to ask those questions. M6 //will do my best to try and root out corruption in this department. M20

VO: While the Minister launched an internal investigation and requested that the auditor-general’s office independently look into possible irregularities, the Standing Committee on Public Accounts, or SCOPA, also launched an enquiry.

HLENGWA: //You are looking at here expenditure which took place within the parameters of the emergency spending protocols because of the COVID19 to disaster. // we don't think the fence was value for money.[from beginning of clip] M1

VO: SCOPA chairman, Mkhuleko Hlengwa, spoke to us via SKYPE from rural KZN.

HLENGWA: /We need to understand whether there was a need for the fence
/ we need to understand fully whether the contract was awarded consistently with the regulation [from end of same clip] M3// We look at the whole value chain M3

VO: Prior to the fence being erected, consultations were held with some local roleplayers – Schoeman, was present at this meeting.

HERMANUS: They it wasn't it wasn't actually A fact finding mission or to decide to do it or not//It was an instruction and it's coming up and that's it. // INT1M17

VO: The Minister has subsequently, aland so questioned the legitimacy of the contract and the quality of the fence.

DE LILLE: We can't be pyaing thirty seven million then at the end of the day. M22 // that in itself you know shows that you must've been bought a very expensive type of wire. And why is it possible that even as we speak now a lot of the fense has been cut through, M12

VO: Magwa Construction declined an interview prior to the investigation being concluded, but sent the following in writing:

The company has “responded to all the Special Investigation Units queries.”

He further stated that “The tender rates are competitive market related rates” and that “The final contract amount will be a lot less than R37 million” in response to the allegation that the fence was overpriced.

VO: The investigation into possible abuse of COVID-19 disaster funding is a priority for SCOPA, assures Hlengwa.

HLENGWA: // we have aslways said as SCOPA, pulbic accoutns is also about the quality of work that comes out of the expenditure the public can't be expected to be footing bills were nonsensical shoddy work M15

VO: With regards to the effectiveness of the fence, Magwa Construction stated: “We were appointed to construct a fence within a 4 week period according to the specifications supplied by the Department of Public Works. That is exactly what we did.”

Security Expert Cilliers explains border security goes beyond a razor wire fence.

JAKKIE: // an engagement with the simplest security expert would have told them that building a fence without having observation on that fence without patrolling it without having motion detectors and other things is just a complete waste of time and money. Int3M4

HLENGWA: // where we find that things did not go consistent with the law, consequence management must be undertaken by the department and the law enforcement agencies LAST CLIP ON TIMELINE

VO: A move Minister De Lille fully supports.

DE LILLE: / /we will make an example of those who are alleged to be involved in this. // corruption steals from the poor. Corru[tion impact on service delivery. M13

VO: But delivering proper border security will require a multi-disciplinary approach – explains Cilliers.

JAKKIE: There's no single magic bullet in resolving our border insecurity challenge. // We need to fix the military. We need to fix the police. We need to fix home affairs and we need to make them work together. INT3M1


PROMOS

PROMO 1
VO: A multi-million rand border repair project between Zimbabwe & South Africa was commissioned in response to COVID-19 – but it appears to makes no difference to opportunistic smugglers. We investigate.

PROMO 2
VO: Government awarded a R37-million tender to fix the border fence between Zimbabwe and South Africa. Meant to restrict movement and the spread of COVID-19, things haven't quite gone according to plan.

PROMO 3
VO: COVID-19 travel bans shut South Africa’s borders to all non-essential movement. Millions were spent on an emergency fence repair project. But is it effective and did we get what we paid for?

metadata.Further information: Construction of a new fence at the Beitbridge border between South Africa and Zimbabwe will begin this week and be completed within 40 days, public works minister Patricia de Lille said on Thursday. "In terms of Section 27 (2) (l) of the Disaster Management Act, No. 57 of 2002, I have invoked emergency procurement procedures in relation to the erection and repairs of the border fences, east and west of the (Beitbridge) border post," De Lille said at the time. The step followed President Cyril Ramaphosa’s address to the nation when he declared a national State of Disaster in response to the Covid-19 pandemic, saying the country's borders would be secured, and the Department of Defence had asked that the fence be repaired for the shutdown. However, in May, De Lille said the newly erected fence had been damaged, and that units of the SANDF were being deployed to the border. The R37m fence at the Beitbridge border separating SA and Zimbabwe was hardly up a day before trespassers cut through it to smuggle in contraband. And the presence of military personnel along the border has done little to repel desperate Zimbabweans and criminals from crossing over to this country. “The fence was hardly up for one day and the crooks came through with cases of cigarettes and smuggling food, and all of that,” an exasperated Patricia de Lille told MPs on Monday. The public works and infrastructure minister told MPs that the auditor-general confirmed on Thursday that he will investigate whether SA got value for money from the project and whether due processes were followed in appointing the contractor to erect the fence. “But it's going to take longer due to the lockdown,” De Lille was told. “What must be condemned in the strongest possible terms is the criminality that is taking place in our borders. The crooks are always one [step] ahead of us and where we were asked to replace the fence was specifically where they call it the hotspots.” She said she asked defence minister Nosiviwe Mapisa-Nqakula on April 4, to make the SA national defence force available to patrol the fence regularly. “Even that is not helping,” said De Lille. “They are watching them. The SANDF is there on bikes, they drive up there, but the crooks just know where and when to strike. It is big problem at our borders that we need to address going into the future to make sure with the help of other countries, we secure the borders of SA,” she added. It was the first time that a parliamentary committee discussed the controversial fence which was erected as a measure to fight the spread of coronavirus. An audit into the procurement process of the Beitbridge border fence is underway. The Public Works and Infrastructure Department says it has already paid around R21-million for the fence. But pictures of the damaged fence has been making the rounds on social media. Officials have reported problems of vandalism. The project is estimated to cost R37-million while the actual cost of the fence will be determined when the project is complete. We interview Security Expert working on the border, the CPF chairperson and two Zim smugglers bringing food and smokes.
